The resort booking closed at midnight, and Gurleen was sure she already knew the answer. A two-day trek, tents, a bonfire: she'd have loved it, so surely everyone would. Nilesh was ready to pay the deposit.
"Give me one hour," she said. She sent the team a short anonymous poll with three options and a line: "Tell me honestly, nothing is decided." Then she walked over to Farah and Dinesh, who rarely spoke up in meetings, and asked them directly.
By eleven the results were in. Only four of fourteen wanted the trek. Two had small children, one had a bad knee, and several simply wanted to be home by night. Gurleen laughed at herself. "I'd have booked a trip for me and three others."
They chose the day trip to the lake. Nilesh paid the deposit at 11:40.

qa.q: How many of the fourteen wanted the trek?
qa.a: Only four of fourteen.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel when the poll results came in?
qa.a: She was amused rather than defensive, realising she'd imagined everyone wanted what she wanted, and she treated the surprise as useful.

qa.q: Which of Gurleen's steps worked best, and why?
qa.a: The anonymous poll plus asking Farah and Dinesh directly, because quieter people and those with reasons like children or a bad knee got heard.

qa.q: How might Farah feel being asked directly?
qa.a: Farah might feel noticed and more willing to say what suits them, having rarely spoken up in meetings.

grounding: It shows a woman under a deadline checking what her team actually wants, seeking out quieter colleagues, and learning from the surprise.

passage:
Alka had run the tiny momo counter in a Guwahati market for three months, and she made the chutney the way she loved it: fiery, with bhut jolokia. "Everyone likes it hot," Bhupen said, stirring the pot. "You and me both."
But Alka had noticed some plates coming back half-full. On Saturday she stuck a small card on the counter: "Too spicy? Not spicy enough? Tell me!" She also asked the college students, the office workers and an old couple who came every Sunday, not just the regulars who were her friends.
The old couple said the chutney made them cough. Two students wanted a milder sauce for dipping.
"Huh," Alka said, surprised, then pleased. "We've been cooking for the two of us."
The next week there were two bowls on the counter, one red, one pale green.

qa.q: What did Alka's card on the counter say?
qa.a: "Too spicy? Not spicy enough? Tell me!"

qa.q: Why was Alka surprised, then pleased, by the answers?
qa.a: She'd assumed most people liked the chutney as hot as she did, and the answers showed her something she could fix to serve more people. 😊

qa.q: Why was it smart of Alka to ask the old couple and the students, not only her friends?
qa.a: Her friends share her taste, so only people unlike her could show who the chutney was putting off.

qa.q: How does the change affect the old couple who come every Sunday?
qa.a: They now have a milder option and can enjoy their momos without coughing, and may feel their visits matter.

grounding: It shows a woman checking what customers actually think, asking people unlike herself, and treating the surprise as a chance to learn.

passage:
"Wait, you're for the vendor ban on MG Road?" Afreen put her chai down. "I thought everyone our age was against it."
Zubin shrugged. "Not everyone."
"Okay. I'm surprised, which probably means I only talk to people who think like me. Tell me why."
"You really want to know, or you want to argue?"
"Want to know. I'll argue later." She grinned.
"My bike shop is on that road. Customers can't park, an ambulance got stuck there last month, and the shops pay rent the vendors don't."
"Hm. I didn't think about the ambulance."
"And you?"
"The vendors are families. Some have been there thirty years."
"That's fair too."
Afreen tapped her phone. "Would you come with me to ask a couple of the vendors? And I'll come and ask your neighbours."
"Deal. Ammi will think we've gone mad, agreeing to listen."

qa.q: Where is Zubin's bike shop?
qa.a: On that road, MG Road, where the vendor ban is planned.

qa.q: What does Afreen think her surprise tells her?
qa.a: She thinks it probably means she only talks to people who think like her, so she treats it as a reason to ask rather than argue.

qa.q: What plan do Afreen and Zubin make, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: To ask a couple of the vendors and Zubin's neighbours together, so both of them hear directly from people on each side.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when Afreen asks to understand instead of arguing?
qa.a: Zubin might feel respected and more open to Afreen's side, which shows when Zubin calls her point about the vendors fair.

grounding: It shows a woman who, surprised by her sibling's view, asks what they think and plans to hear people unlike herself.

passage:
Last spring I was put in charge of the new night-shift break room at our call centre in Mohali. I'm Revathi, the first woman shift lead there, and I was sure I knew what people wanted: a quiet room, soft lights, a shelf of books, herbal tea. That's what I'd want.
Before ordering, I made myself do two things. I sent a three-question form to all sixty people on nights. And I sat for two evenings with the people least like me: Naveen and Suraj from the billing floor, who are loud, play cricket on their phones and have never, I think, touched herbal tea.
The replies surprised me. Most people wanted a microwave, a carrom board and a phone-charging strip. Books came last. My first feeling was a little hurt, honestly. Then I thought: if it surprises me, I've learned something.
We got the microwave and the carrom board. The room is never empty now.

qa.q: How many people on nights did Revathi send the form to?
qa.a: All sixty people on nights.

qa.q: What did Revathi feel when the replies came in, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt a little hurt that her idea came last, then treated the surprise as a sign she had learned something about her colleagues.

qa.q: Which choice made the break room work?
qa.a: Checking what people actually wanted with the form and by sitting with colleagues unlike her, instead of ordering what she herself would enjoy.

qa.q: How might Naveen and Suraj experience the new break room?
qa.a: Naveen and Suraj probably feel noticed and welcome, since they were asked, and the room now has the carrom board and microwave people like them wanted.

grounding: It shows a mature person checking what others actually think, seeking out people unlike herself, and treating surprise at disagreement as a chance to learn.

passage:
Operations manager's note, March (Anand)
Disha, 24, took over the packing team leader role last month. Her first big decision was which two days the team would work from the warehouse office.
She told me she assumed everyone wanted Mondays and Fridays at home, as she does. She didn't act on that. She spoke to each of the fourteen people, including the older supervisors on the loading dock whom she rarely works with.
The answers surprised her. Most of the dock staff wanted to come in on Fridays, because that's when the trucks are loaded and questions come up. Two young parents wanted Wednesdays at home for school pickup.
When she brought me the plan, she said, "I was completely wrong about what people want, which is good to know now." She set Wednesdays and Mondays at home.
Next: I've asked her to share how she ran those conversations with the other team leads.

qa.q: How many people did Disha speak to?
qa.a: She spoke to each of the fourteen people.

qa.q: How did Disha feel about being wrong, and what shows it?
qa.a: She seemed calm and even glad, saying she was completely wrong about what people want, "which is good to know now".

qa.q: Which step in Disha's approach helped most, and why?
qa.a: Talking to the loading-dock supervisors she rarely works with, because their need to be in on truck-loading Fridays was exactly what her own assumption had missed.

qa.q: How might the two young parents feel about the final plan?
qa.a: They are likely relieved and grateful, since Wednesdays at home fit their school pickups and someone actually asked them.

grounding: It shows a mature person checking what others actually think, reaching out to those unlike herself, and treating surprise as a sign to learn.

passage:
Wednesday
Almost booked karaoke for the team outing today. I love karaoke, my friends love karaoke, and I was ready to call it the obvious choice. Then I remembered last year's picnic, which I planned for "everyone", and half the team didn't come. So I ran a quick anonymous poll instead. Karaoke came fourth! First was a cooking class, which I'd never have guessed. That surprise bugged me, in a good way.
I went to Deepika's desk, since she's the quietest in the team and nothing like me, and asked what she'd actually enjoy. She said most of the older staff dread singing in public, and a few can't stay late because of their kids. I had never thought of that once.
Cooking class it is, on a Saturday morning. Note to self: when I'm sure, ask.
Mahima

qa.q: What came first in the team poll?
qa.a: A cooking class came first.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel about the poll result, and why does that matter?
qa.a: Mahima felt surprised and a little bugged, in a good way; treating that surprise as a sign of not knowing the team led to asking Deepika.

qa.q: Which of Mahima's choices made the outing fit the team better?
qa.a: Running an anonymous poll and then asking Deepika, someone quite unlike Mahima, brought out the dread of singing and the need for a morning slot.

qa.q: How might the older staff feel about a Saturday-morning cooking class compared with karaoke?
qa.a: They would likely feel more comfortable and included, since they dread singing in public and some can't stay late.

grounding: Shows a young professional checking what colleagues actually want, seeking out someone quite different, and using the surprise to learn.

passage: Vandana had driven the library van into Sangole every Thursday for a month, the shelves full of the English novels she had loved at college. Almost nobody borrowed them. Her first thought was that the town didn't read. Then she stopped herself: that was a guess, and she'd been wrong before. So on the fifth Thursday she parked by the bangle shop and simply asked. Ritu, who ran the shop and had left school at fourteen, laughed. "Who has time for fat books? Give us short stories in Marathi. And something on sewing patterns." A group of college boys asked for exam guides. An old man wanted newspapers read aloud. Vandana wrote it all in a notebook, a little stung and very curious. The next month the van carried half its shelves in Marathi, and a queue formed before she had parked.

qa.q: Where did Vandana park on the fifth Thursday?
qa.a: She parked by the bangle shop.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling as she wrote down the requests?
qa.a: Vandana felt a little stung but very curious, treating the surprise as information about what people actually want.

qa.q: Which choice turned the library van around?
qa.a: Dropping the guess that the town didn't read and asking people like Ritu directly, then changing the shelves to match.

qa.q: How might Ritu see the library van now?
qa.a: Ritu would likely feel listened to, seeing Marathi stories on the shelves after being asked, rather than books chosen for someone else.

grounding: Shows a young worker asking townspeople unlike herself what they want instead of assuming, and learning from the surprise.

passage: Hana was planning the team retreat for her design studio in Kyoto. Her first thought was a mountain hike and hot springs; she loved both, and surely everyone did. She almost booked it. Then she caught herself. Did she actually know? She sent a short, anonymous survey to all twelve people. Before looking at the answers, she wrote down her guess: ten would want the hike. Then she went further. She asked Ada, the newest member, from Lisbon, and the two oldest designers what they'd enjoy. The results surprised her. Only four wanted the hike. Three had knee problems. Most wanted a cooking class and a museum. Hana laughed at her own guess. "Ten!" she said to Ada. "I was so sure." Ada smiled. "Thanks for asking. I'd never have said anything."

qa.q: How many people wanted the hike in the survey?
qa.a: Only four wanted the hike.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when she saw the results?
qa.a: She felt surprised and a little amused at herself, laughing at how sure she had been.

qa.q: What did Hana do that others could copy?
qa.a: She wrote down her guess, sent an anonymous survey, and asked people unlike herself before deciding, treating her surprise as a lesson.

qa.q: How might Ada feel about being asked?
qa.a: Ada seemed grateful and relieved, since she would never have spoken up on her own.

grounding: Shows a mature team lead checking what others actually think, seeking people unlike herself, and treating surprise as a sign to learn.

passage: At the Bengaluru school, Arohi, the new Class 8 coordinator, was sure all parents wanted more homework. Her own parents had, and her teacher friends agreed. She drafted a notice to double it. Then she paused. She asked the vice-principal, Neelam ma'am, "Do we actually know what parents think?" Neelam ma'am shook her head. So Arohi set up a short form and, more importantly, stood at the gate at pickup time for three days, asking parents she'd never spoken to. A father who drove an auto said his son already worked till nine. A mother who worked night shifts said she couldn't help with more. Some did want more. Most wanted less but better. Arohi was surprised, and a little embarrassed. At the staff meeting she said, "I was wrong about what parents think. Here's what they said."

qa.q: How many days did Arohi stand at the gate at pickup time?
qa.a: For three days.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she heard the parents' answers?
qa.a: She felt surprised and a little embarrassed, because she had been sure all parents wanted more homework.

qa.q: Which step made Arohi's decision fairer?
qa.a: Talking to parents she had never spoken to at the gate, not just her own circle, before changing the homework policy.

qa.q: How might the mother who works night shifts see the new approach?
qa.a: She might feel heard and relieved, since more homework would have been hard for her to support.

grounding: Shows a young coordinator checking what parents actually think, seeking people unlike herself, and treating surprise as a chance to learn.

passage:
Dear Jatin,
Before you finalise the new app design, I want to share something I learned the hard way.
Last month I was sure our users wanted a dark, minimal look. Everyone in our team liked it, and I did too. I nearly signed off. Then I asked myself: who do we actually know who uses this app? We're all twenty-something designers. Our users include shopkeepers, grandparents and farmers.
So I went out. I sat with a kirana owner in Jayanagar, a retired teacher, and two women at a self-help group meeting. Almost all of them wanted bigger buttons and brighter colours. I was stunned. Then I was grateful.
Could we test your design with five people who aren't like us before we launch? I'll help set it up.
Best,
Rukmini

qa.q: Who did Rukmini sit with to test the app?
qa.a: A kirana owner in Jayanagar, a retired teacher, and two women at a self-help group meeting.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling on hearing what users wanted?
qa.a: Rukmini was stunned at first, then grateful, seeing that the team's taste was not the users' taste.

qa.q: What does Rukmini suggest to Jatin, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Testing the design with five people unlike the team before launch, because the team's own preferences may not match its users.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Jatin might feel a little defensive about the design, but also relieved to have a clear, practical way to check it.

grounding: A letter shows a young designer checking what users actually think, seeking people unlike the team, and treating surprise as a chance to learn.

passage:
Sarika, you asked how I got better at my job this year. Honestly? I stopped trusting my own head. I'm Anjali, and I design sign-up forms for a bank.
Last spring I was sure everyone hated long forms. I hate them, my team hates them. So I built a one-page sign-up. Then I made myself do something uncomfortable: I sat in a branch in Lucknow for two days and asked customers, mostly older people and small shopkeepers, to try it.
Half of them wanted more steps, not fewer. One man said, "When it's too quick, I feel it's a trick." I was genuinely shocked. And then I thought: that shock is the most useful thing that's happened to me all year.
Now, whenever I'm surprised by what someone thinks, I write it in a little notebook. Surprise means I was assuming. The notebook is nearly full.

qa.q: Where did Anjali sit for two days?
qa.a: Anjali sat in a branch in Lucknow for two days.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when half the customers wanted more steps?
qa.a: Anjali felt genuinely shocked, then curious and grateful, seeing the surprise as a useful sign of an assumption.

qa.q: What habit does Anjali keep, and why does it help?
qa.a: Writing down every surprise in a notebook, because each one shows where Anjali was assuming others think the same way.

qa.q: What was the one-page form like for the man who felt it was a trick?
qa.a: The quick form made the man uneasy and distrustful, because speed itself felt suspicious.

grounding: Shows a young professional who checks what people unlike the design team actually think and treats surprise at disagreement as a sign to learn.

passage:
I'm Yamini, and I sat next to Lalremsiami for a year at the youth NGO in Aizawl, so I watched this happen.
We were planning a health camp for young people. In the first meeting, most of us, all in our twenties, agreed it should be on a Saturday. "Everyone's free on Saturdays," someone said, and we moved on.
Lalremsiami didn't move on. She wrote "Saturday?" on a sticky note. The next week I saw her in the market talking to a vegetable seller's son, then two girls from the church choir, then a boy who works at the car wash. She came back looking surprised, almost pleased.
"Saturday is their busiest day," she told us. "Sunday after church works for most of them."
Some of us were a bit annoyed about redoing the posters. But the camp was full. I still don't know exactly what went on in her head, but she seemed to enjoy being wrong.

qa.q: Which day did most of the team first choose for the camp?
qa.a: Most of the team agreed the camp should be on a Saturday.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami seem to feel after talking to people in the market?
qa.a: Lalremsiami seemed surprised and almost pleased, as if finding out she was wrong felt like useful news.

qa.q: Why was talking to people in the market a wise step?
qa.a: It checked what the young people actually needed, showing Saturday was their busiest day, instead of assuming the team's free day was everyone's.

qa.q: How did some of the team feel about changing the day?
qa.a: Some felt a bit annoyed about redoing the posters, though the full camp showed the change was worth it.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's account, a young woman who checks what others actually think and treats surprise as a sign to learn.

passage:
Monday. Nikita planned her first homework for Class 8: watch a short video at home and answer three questions online. "Every kid has a phone these days," said Santosh, the other new teacher. Nikita nodded, then paused. She wrote one line in her planner: Ask first.
Tuesday. She handed out slips: How do you usually do homework? Own phone, family phone, no phone, no internet. Tick one. No names.
Thursday. She counted the slips in the staffroom. Eleven out of thirty-four had no phone of their own. Six had no internet at home at all.
"Huh," Santosh said, reading over her shoulder. "I'd have bet on everyone."
"So would I," Nikita said, looking more curious than embarrassed. She printed the three questions on paper, put the video on the school library computer, and wrote a new note to herself: surprise means ask again.

qa.q: How many students had no internet at home at all?
qa.a: Six students had no internet at home at all.

qa.q: Why did Nikita pause after Santosh's comment?
qa.a: Nikita felt cautious and a little unsure, wanting to check how students really do homework instead of assuming everyone had a phone.

qa.q: How does Nikita adjust the homework, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Nikita prints the questions and puts the video on the school library computer, so students without phones or internet can still do it.

qa.q: How does Santosh react to the slips?
qa.a: Santosh is surprised, having bet that everyone had a phone, and seems to learn alongside Nikita.

grounding: Shows a young teacher who asks instead of assuming, and treats a surprising answer as a reason to learn and adjust.

passage: Ankita, you're about to announce the new flexi-time plan assuming everyone wants it. Let me tell you what happened to your Indu didi at twenty-five, when I ran the staff welfare committee at the textile mill. I was sure everyone wanted the canteen to serve lunch later, because all my friends on the design floor ate late. Before posting the notice, something made me walk down to the loom floor and the packing unit and simply ask. The weavers wanted lunch earlier, because their shift started at six. The packers didn't care about timing at all; they wanted the canteen to stop running out of rice. I was surprised, even a bit embarrassed. So I treated the surprise as a clue and asked more questions. We ended up with two lunch slots and more rice. Ask first, Ankita. It saves a lot of notices.

qa.q: Why did the weavers want lunch earlier?
qa.a: Because their shift started at six.

qa.q: How did young Indu feel on hearing what the weavers and packers wanted?
qa.a: Indu felt surprised and a bit embarrassed, then curious, treating the surprise as a clue to learn more.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the canteen plan work?
qa.a: Walking down to the loom floor and the packing unit to ask before posting the notice, which led to two lunch slots and more rice.

qa.q: What did the packers care about most?
qa.a: The packers didn't mind the timing; they wanted the canteen to stop running out of rice.

grounding: Shows a person checking what others actually think, seeking out people unlike themselves, and treating surprise at disagreement as a sign to learn.
